events.title: BME 280B Seminar: Dr. Jeff Hasty – “Engineered cellular differentiation in physiologically relevant environments”
events.description:
Welcome to the 6th week of our BME 280B seminar series, a weekly seminar covering topics of current research in computational biology and bioinformatics.

Open to all, food is provided. Class enrollment is not required.

Please join us this week to learn more about the works of Dr. Jeff Hasty:

Title of Talk: Engineered cellular differentiation in physiologically relevant environments

Presenter: Dr. Jeff Hasty, Professor of Bioengineering and Molecular Biology and Director of the Synthetic Biology Institute, University of California, San Diego

Description: The original defining approach to synthetic biology is the use of mathematical models to design and construct gene circuits. This engineering approach has guided our recent work on the synchronized lysis circuit (SLC), a quorum-sensing program that drives a bacterial population to grow, lyse, and release a payload in cycles, turning tumor-colonizing bacteria into a self-dosing bioreactor. In two-dimensional culture the SLC cycles with a period near 5 hr, while in animals that period is roughly 24 hr. I will first describe a measurement platform we built to ascertain how the physiological environment changes circuit behavior.The device has two layers and permits tuning of oxygen levels, matrix composition, gradients, and co-culture independently at tissue scale while imaging single colonies. I will then describe a general design theme that focuses on plasmid replication as opposed to transcription. If two plasmids in a cell share one origin(dupORI), a single controller limits both, so one gains copies only as the other loses them. A simple model captures this: the total copy number settles to a fixed value, but the split between the two plasmid types is free to drift, and cell division and the noise in replication spread a clonal population across a range of plasmid configurations. With environmental pressure, a single strain tunes the relative abundance of plasmid types to maximize growth, and this principle can be used to engineer differentiation within a clonal population. I will close with two designs we are currently testing. In the first, the two plasmids of a dupORI pair cut each other, with colicin selection holding the balance, so the strain can switch between discrete states and retain them as a type of read/write circuit. In the second, one strain runs two separate lysis circuits that take turns, delivering two payloads sequentially.

Bio: Jeff Hasty received his Ph.D. in physics from the Georgia Institute of Technology in 1997, where he learned how to do science from his advisor Kurt Wiesenfeld. He was subsequently a postdoctoral fellow at Boston University, where he learned engineering from Jim Collins (’98– ’01). Somewhere during his postdoctoral stay with Jim he mutated from a theoretical physicist into a hybrid computational/molecular biologist. He is currently at the University of California, San Diego, where he holds the Paul A. Libby Endowed Chair and is a Professor in the Departments of Bioengineering and Molecular Biology, and Director of the Synthetic Biology Institute. Cells, constructs, and microfluidic devices from his lab are in use for research and teaching around the world and he is known for freely sharing genetic constructs and measurement technologies that “just work.”

Hosted by: Professor of Applied Mathematics, Dr. Marcella M. Gomez

The Biomolecular Engineering (BME) Department within the Baskin School of Engineering features an interdisciplinary blend of engineering, biology, chemistry, and statistics designed to foster collaboration with other departments. This blend reflects our vision of the direction that biomedical discovery will take over the next two decades.

The Genomics Institute at UC Santa Cruz bridges disciplinary gaps to apply the combined power of engineering, mathematics, and the biological and physical sciences to create innovations that will improve our world making concrete impacts on human health and conservation. As an academic institute, we are also dedicated to broadening STEM education both locally and globally to raise up a diverse generation of scientists to lead the genomic revolution that promises to save lives and preserve our planet. We are committed to openly and responsibly sharing what we create to unite global communities.

events.title: Carlos Motta: When Time Stands Still
events.description:
Carlos Motta’s When Time Stands Still, the artist’s second solo show with the IAS, features new and recent installations, videos, and sculptures highlighting the artist’s preoccupation with the historical and aesthetic productions of difference and marginalization that shape the present.

The selection of artworks in the exhibition explore the unsettling experience of living in a time that seems violently stuck on repeat. Archetypal figures from art history (a fool, a siren, a witness, a victim) reappear in the current moment as containers of time, bringing the past of imperialism, colonization, and displacement into a present marked by the rise of anti-immigration politics, climate injustice, and other forms of disposability. Some works challenge this violent repetition of time. The clock moves, if gruelingly, in an endurance-based video performance, No One, 2025. For forty-six minutes, the artist undertakes to keep his eyes open, witnessing, withstanding, confronting, and resisting the bombardment of images, both historical and otherwise, that normalize harm. In another video work, Gravity, 2024, performers enact rescue carries, supporting each other until they can’t bear the weight. Together, the artworks act as a proposal about how to rethink time—how to slow time—with a poetic and aesthetic cadence that might counter the numbing reverberations of living in the present.

When Time Stands Still is organized as part of Visualizing Abolition, an arts-based initiative that reaches across prison borders to create a future free of prisons.

Carlos Motta (b. 1978, Colombia) is a multidisciplinary artist whose work has been shown widely nationally and internationally. Solo exhibitions venues include the Museu d’Art Contemporani de Barcelona; Nikolaj Kunsthal, Copenhagen; Museo de Arte Moderno de Bogotá; Wexner Center for the Arts, Columbus, OH ; Röda Sten Konsthall, Gothenburg, Sweden; Galeria Vermelho, São Paulo; Pérez Art Museum Miami (PAMM); Tate Modern, London; and New Museum, New York (2012). He has also participated in major biennials, including the Venice Biennale; Berlin Biennale; Bienal de São Paulo; and the Gwangju Biennale. Motta is Associate Professor of Interdisciplinary Art, Fine Arts Department, Pratt Institute, Brooklyn.

events.title: Victor ‘Marka27’ Quiñonez: Ni de Aquí, Ni de Allá
events.description:
Organized in partnership with the Center for Art and Advocacy, located in Brooklyn, New York, Ni de Aquí, Ni de Allá (Not From Here, Not From There) by multidisciplinary artist Victor ‘Marka27’ Quiñonez features a wide range of artworks  that issue a bold declaration of dual belonging, including altars, an elaborately immersive botanica, paintings referencing visual symbolism drawn from textiles, graffiti and community traditions, and, in a series called I.C.E. Scream, large, brightly colored resin sculptures in the shape of melting Mexican paletas (popsicles). As the exhibition title suggests (a phrase widely used in bilingual and bicultural communities), these artworks reflect the artist’s interest in the experience of living between worlds even as violent notions of nationalism and identity pervade. 

Accompanying the exhibition, Elevar la Cultura, an immersive sculptural installation featuring a twenty-two-foot-tall pyramid built from ice coolers adorned with ancestral textiles, sacred symbols, and mural work will be on view at Santa Cruz Barrios Unidos (1817 Soquel) November 7, 2026- March 7, 2027. As Quiñonez explains, this sculpture epitomizes the contradictions of living—and laboring—as an immigrant in the United States: 

 “Most people see the cooler as a tool for leisure…for barbecues, tailgating, and celebrations. But for immigrant communities, the cooler is a tool and symbol for opportunity and independence. In every major city, you see families and vendors selling fruit, food, and water out of these coolers on the streets and in subway stations. They’re a necessity for survival and a way to start an honest living,” the artist shares.

The Institute of Arts and Sciences will be the second venue to successfully present Ni de Aquí, Ni de Allá to the public. First organized by Boston University Art Galleries and curated by Kate Fowle in September of 2025, the exhibition debuted to critical acclaim before gaining national attention after its abrupt removal from its second venue, the University of North Texas, where it had been installed just one week prior to it being censored. 

Victor ‘Marka27’ Quiñonez is a renowned international visual artist who is known for his diverse works that intersect contemporary art, graffiti, vinyl toys, fashion and design and art activism. Quiñonez has exhibited globally and collaborated with major brands while creating landmark public art in cities across the U.S. He is a Frieze Los Angeles Impact Prize winner (2025) and a Right of Return and Art for Justice Fellow (2023, 2024).

events.title: Aesthetic Breach: Past and Present Struggles for Justice in North African Comics
events.description:
This exhibition brings together comics and graphic narratives from Egypt, Tunisia, Algeria, and Morocco, introducing a broad range of contemporary artists while centering the works of Sadri Khiari, a major figure of the antiracist left in Tunisia and France, and Salim Zerrouki, an Algerian cartoonist whose drawings combine ferocious satire and nostalgia. Across different forms, styles, and perspectives, these works engage questions of justice, memory, colonial and postcolonial histories, gender, migration, language, political struggle, and everyday life.

The artwork selected for this exhibition depicts complex social realities and historical trajectories, while personalizing global issues such as racist violence or societal collapse. Zerrouki’s Rwama chronicles the collapse of Algeria’s post-independence social order through daily life in an Algiers apartment complex. Khiari’s Toussaint est mort dans sa tombe reaches beyond North Africa to trace what happened to the body of Haitian revolutionary leader Toussaint Louverture after his death in French captivity.

The exhibition also asks us to pay attention to comics as form—to how these stories are told and why that matters. Speech balloons and panels offer ways to narrate intimate experiences, everyday life, and social issues. Indeed, graphic novels can be an entry into grassroots perspectives and individual experiences of subjection and resistance. Bringing comics into the gallery also draws attention to their visual and material qualities—to drawing and text, panels and sequences, composition and rhythm. 

The Eloise Pickard Smith Gallery is a teaching gallery at UC Santa Cruz. This exhibition was developed in collaboration with Thomas Serres and the Center for the Middle East and North Africa. Curated by Faculty Director Susana Ruiz, curatorial intern Annelise Schouten, and the gallery team, with Simona Gabrieli as guest co-curator. With support from The Humanities Institute, Employing Humanities, and Jim Gunderson.

Reception: Nov 6, 2026 — 3 to 5pm at the Eloise Pickard Smith Gallery at Cowell College.

events.title: Protect Your Soil in Heavy Rain: Actionable Strategies for Wet Weather
events.description:
With El Niño expected to bring significant rainfall this season, safeguarding your garden’s foundation is more critical than ever. Join the UC Master Gardeners and the UCSC Center for Agroecology for a timely, practical workshop dedicated to protecting and preserving your garden soil during severe wet weather.

In this fast-paced, FREE online session, three experienced Master Gardeners will deliver actionable strategies to help you manage your landscape. We will quickly cover key topics to maximize our time, leaving plenty of room for your specific questions.

Core Topics Covered

  • Improving Drainage: Practical methods to prevent waterlogging and keep roots healthy.
  • Directing Water Flow: How to safely channel excess runoff away from vulnerable areas.
  • Protecting the Soil Surface: Effective techniques to shield your topsoil from heavy impact.
  • Preventing Erosion: Strategic solutions to stop runoff from washing your valuable soil away.

events.title: Reckoning with Redress: The Legacy of Japanese American Incarceration
events.description:
Forty-five years ago, survivors and descendants of the WWII Japanese American incarceration, testified before the Commission on Wartime Relocation and Internment of Civilians (CWRIC), helping set in motion what would become one of the largest reparations efforts in U.S. history. This year’s Peggy Downes Baskin Ethics lecture marks that anniversary with the launch and premiere of Reckoning with Redress (RWR) — a new cinematic digital history project, along with the lecture “A Debt Owed–Korematsu, Reparations, and the Ever-Recycling Racial Pathology of 1619,” given by Donald Tamaki. Produced by Full Spectrum Features Education, in partnership with Humanities Dean Jasmine Alinder, RWR is an Open Educational Resource, which includes a film (Enough), an immersive game, and an interactive learning website, that explores the history and legacies of the Japanese American Redress Movement.

Join us to learn more about this important moment in history and explore these valuable learning resources.

Doors will open for light refreshments at 5:30pm. Program begins at 6:00pm.

This event is free and open to the public. Seating is first come, first served.

Parking Information

The Cultural Center Merrill College is located in Merrill College, in the northeast corner of the campus core. Those walking or arriving by Metro bus or campus shuttle can take the steep path heading northeast from the Crown/Merrill bus stop.

For those driving from the Main Entrance, stay on Coolidge Drive. Shortly after Coolidge turns left and becomes McLaughlin Drive, turn right at the sign for Merrill College. At the top of the hill, veer right. There is parking for “A,” “B,” and “C” permits along the right. Parking is provided free of charge courtesy of the Humanities Division. There are two accessible parking spaces if you turn left at the top of the hill and two more if you turn right. Parking attendants will be on site to issue parking permits to event attendees.

Donald Tamaki is a Senior Counsel at the San Francisco law firm of Minami Tamaki LLP having received his BA and JD from U.C. Berkeley.

In the 1980’s, Tamaki served on the pro bono legal team that reopened the 1944 Supreme Court case of Fred Korematsu, a notorious precedent that validated forcing 125,000 Japanese Americans into concentration camps on the claim they were spies. But almost 40 years later, secret intelligence reports and Justice Department memos surfaced, categorically denying that Japanese Americans were spying, admitting there was no reason for the mass removal, and calling the Army’s claims “intentional falsehoods.” Despite whistle-blower protests from government lawyers urging that they had a duty not to lie to the Court, the Solicitor General stood by the Army’s claims knowing they were fabricated. The evidence was suppressed, and much of it ordered burned. On the basis that a fraud had been committed, Korematsu’s criminal conviction was erased. The ruling boosted the call for reparations to redress this great wrong.

In 2021, California Governor Gavin Newsom appointed Tamaki to serve on the nine-member California Reparations Task Force (the Task Force) that produced the groundbreaking Final Report comprehensively documenting the cumulative impact of 246 years of enslavement, another 100 years of Jim Crow oppression, and decades more of segregation, and to recommend to the Legislature what California should do to address the resulting compounding and cascading harms.

Tamaki is part of the leadership team of the Alliance for Reparations, Reconciliation, and Truth (ARRT), a multi-racial statewide coalition working to promote public awareness of the harms wrought by racial subjugation, and to transform the Task Force’s 115 recommendations into legislation.

His awards include the ABA Spirit of Excellence Award (2020), the National Asian Pacific Bar Association Trailblazer Award (2003), and the State Bar of California Loren Miller Award (1987).

The Peggy Downes Baskin Ethics Lecture Series is a lively forum for the discussion and exploration of ethics-related challenges in human endeavors. The Ethics Lecture is made possible by the Peggy Downes Baskin Humanities Endowment for Interdisciplinary Ethics which enables the Humanities Division to promote a dialogue about ethics and ethics related challenges in an interdisciplinary setting. The endowment was established in honor of Peggy Downes Baskin’s longtime interest in ethical issues across the academic spectrum.

This event is open to all students, faculty, staff, and members of the public consistent with University policy and state and federal law.

events.title: CSE Colloquium – One Developer, Two Decades, and Thirty Million Users Later: How Python Tutor Became a Long-Lasting and Widely-Used Academic Software Project
events.description:
Presenter: Philip Guo, UCSD

Abstract:

Since 2010 I have been developing Python Tutor (https://pythontutor.com/), a tool that lets users write code in a web browser and see what happens step-by-step as the computer runs it. The tool visualizes variables, objects, pointers, data structures, and stack frames. These visuals help students to debug their homework, teachers to explain concepts, and programmers to prepare for job interviews. Despite its name, this tool visualizes code written in Python, Java, C, C++, and JavaScript, which are five of the most popular languages used in both teaching and industry.

Throughout the past two decades, nearly 30 million students and teachers from over 180 countries have used Python Tutor to visualize nearly a billion pieces of code. In this talk I will reflect upon the design decisions (and non-decisions!) I made along the way to turn a one-off prototype into one of the most widely-used pieces of academic software today. I will cover three eras of Python Tutor’s development: Act I – Inception, the unique conditions that birthed this idea as a grad student side project. Act II – Acceleration, sustaining a decade’s worth of user growth as I began my career as a professor. Act III – Disruption, when Generative AI both threatens the health of this project and may also be what revitalizes it.

Bio:

Philip Guo (https://pg.ucsd.edu/) is a professor of cognitive science at UC San Diego. His research spans human-computer interaction, computing education, and human-centered AI for education. He studies how people learn computer programming and data science, and he builds tools to help people better understand code and data. For instance, his Python Tutor educational tool (https://pythontutor.com/) has been used by nearly 30 million students and teachers from over 180 countries throughout the past two decades. Python Tutor received a UIST Best Paper award and the ACM SIGCSE Test of Time award for long-term impact. His other lines of research have received 10-year long-term impact awards from VL/HCC and ISSTA, along with Best Paper awards at CHI, UIST, SIGCSE, VL/HCC, ICSE, and ISSTA.

Hosted by: Professor Daniel Fremont and Professor Leilani Gilpin
